lesson.title: The Law That Made Unions Legal: The Wagner Act
lesson.summary: The National Labor Relations Act of 1935, known as the Wagner Act, guaranteed workers the right to organize and bargain collectively, reshaping American labor relations for generations.
lesson.body:
Early New Deal law had offered unions only weak protection. Section 7(a) of the 1933 National Industrial Recovery Act had nominally recognized workers' right to organize, but enforcement was inconsistent, and in May 1935 the Supreme Court struck down the entire National Industrial Recovery Act in Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, wiping out even that limited protection.

Senator Robert F. Wagner of New York had pushed for stronger labor law for years, and with the earlier protections gone, his bill gained new urgency. Roosevelt signed the National Labor Relations Act, commonly called the Wagner Act, on July 5, 1935. It created the National Labor Relations Board with real enforcement power: the authority to run union elections, certify unions as workers' legal bargaining representatives, and prosecute employers for unfair labor practices such as firing workers for organizing.

Union membership grew rapidly under this new legal protection. The Wagner Act's guarantees also helped fuel a split within organized labor. The American Federation of Labor had long organized workers by craft and skill, largely leaving mass production industries like steel and automobiles unorganized. In 1935, John L. Lewis led a breakaway group that became the Congress of Industrial Organizations, using the Wagner Act's new protections to organize entire industrial workforces rather than individual trades.

Alongside the Social Security Act, passed the same year, the Wagner Act was a cornerstone of the Second New Deal, moving federal policy from temporary relief toward permanent rules governing the relationship between American workers and employers.
